tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;

`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.

The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points

515	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
516	
517	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
518	
519	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
520	- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
521	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
522	
523	It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).
524	
525	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
526	
527	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
528	~~~~

623	## 1. What changed and why
624	
625	`m CHOOSE n` is the binomial coefficient. On a fixed-size type, a result that does not fit throws `IntegerOverflow` (section 4; P-73 names `CHOOSE`). The compiled path's helpers, which walk now calls too, broke this rule in two ways (the CHOOSE probe, `plan-24/probes/choose.md`, sections 4.2 and 4.3).
626	
627	**Past the safe-bound table, a raw Java exception.**
628	- Each helper first folds `k` to `min(k, n-k)`.
629	- For `n` above its Pascal table, it then indexes a safe-bound table: `maxIntChooseSafeN[k-2]`, 15 entries for `k` = 2 to 16, or `maxLongChooseSafeN[k-2]`, 32 entries for `k` = 2 to 33.
630	- Its guard against a large `k` tested `k > 33` (`ZZ32`) and `kk > 66` (`ZZ64`), which lie past the tables' ends.
631	- So a folded `k` from 17 to 33 on `ZZ32`, or from 34 to 66 on `ZZ64`, threw `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, which no `catch` sees.
632	- Every coefficient in that region overflows. The smallest is `34 CHOOSE 17` = 2,333,606,220 on `ZZ32`, and `68 CHOOSE 34` = 28,453,041,475,240,576,740 on `ZZ64`. At `n` = 67, a `k` of 34 folds to 33, which is inside the table.
633	
634	**A scratch array shared by parallel calls.** Each helper's slow path, `intSlowCautiousChoose` or `longSlowCautiousChoose`, wrote, divided and multiplied one static array. Calls that run at once, as the iterations of a Fortress loop do, corrupted each other. The results were wrong values, a false `IntegerOverflow`, or a raw `UnknownError`.

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
~~~~

`m CHOOSE n` is the binomial coefficient. On a fixed-size type, a result that does not fit throws `IntegerOverflow` (section 4; P-73 names `CHOOSE`). The compiled path's helpers, which walk now calls too, broke this rule in two ways (the CHOOSE probe, `plan-24/probes/choose.md`, sections 4.2 and 4.3).

**Past the safe-bound table, a raw Java exception.**
- Each helper first folds `k` to `min(k, n-k)`.

### Where the text, the brief or the principles split

**1. Way 2b checks a composition, and the transfers are identities (rung H; Question 2).** P-58: "from the step that moves a binding, the compiled checker checks it against the helper's Java signature" (`POSITIONS.md:55`). For H's 76, the checker reads the helper's call wrapped in the transfers, each of which returns its argument (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleUnsignedIntArith.java:230-231`). So the composition passes whatever the helper computes. Skeptic H's program shows it: a binding over `NN32` named to the signed `simpleIntArith.intLT` is refused on the old code ("(ZZ32, ZZ32)->Boolean is not applicable to an argument of type (NN32, NN32)"), and compiles and answers `true` for 2^31 < 1 on the new code; "So a loud static error becomes a quiet value" (`compile-ladder/rung-natives-hard/SKEPTIC.md:112-134`). Walk answers the same (F-299). For the 76, the walk and compiled guards check that each names the unsigned helper, and they do (F-308). For a later binding over these types, only its guard will. The record's Question 2 weighs the four ways by the team's word and the library's form (`CLIMB-BATCH-24.md:90-100`), and the probe by the same and by distance runs (`plan-24/probes/hard-set.md`, sections 4 to 7); neither names this cost. Question 2 was taken at the probe's default under his half-hour rule, "On his review list" (`:92`). Default: as landed. No entry holds it yet (finding 2).

**2. A compile-time refusal became a run-time crash (rung G; row 867; G.skeptic.1).** On the base, the code generator refused a function or method whose own `where` clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, 'Don't know how to compile this kind of FnDecl.'. With the guard's condition gone, it compiles and links, and its compiled call dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.fss:16-21`). The skeptic asks whether to keep refusing that form until the template carries the variable (`PLAN.md:656`). Default: as landed, the deferred `XXX` run pair. A loud failure stays loud, but moves from the compile to the run.

**3. The code generator compiles every header `where` clause, beyond P-151's three forms (rung G; fork 12).** P-151: "Only the `where`-clause forms that the team wrote down are built: conditional extension, a function's or a method's condition, and `AnyList`'s `comprises` clause" (`POSITIONS.md:63`). G dropped the condition at all three guards, so an object's or a trait's own `where` clause on its own static parameters compiles too (`CodeGen.java:4103-4111`, `:5022-5027`; `compiler_tests/WhereBoundObjectCompiled.fss`). The checker already reads an object's own constraint (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/compiler.md:103`), and the code generator emits nothing for any clause, so no new form gets semantics; G's decision 3 says so (`compile-ladder/rung-codegen-where/REPORT.md`, "9. Decisions", 3). Fork 12's default, not consequential by the record (`CLIMB-BATCH-24.md:117`). A reading of P-151's "built" at the code generator, routine, on the forks' item.

**4. Walk reads a method's declaring type by its name (rung W).** The loader takes `self`'s carrier from the declaring type's name, for fifteen types whose names no program can give its own types, and gives `FlatString` and `JavaString` no carrier, since a program can name its types so (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java:81-95`). W improved the planner's text there: on the patch's build, a program's own `object FlatString` with a helper bound to `nativeStrlen` answered 10 (`rung-natives-self/REPORT.md:27`). The cost is item 63: a library binding of a `FlatString` method that names a helper would stop every program at load (`PLAN.md:145`; skeptic W, "For the curator"). Two departures stay, each with its home: a dotted method of a generic trait or object is refused only where an instance's method is made (row 864), and a program's object that extends a carried trait against its `comprises` clause still reaches the helper (row 551; F-299). No default on record for item 63.

**5. The comment's "rewrites the body", and a local function (row 865).** The revised comment says "The compiler, before type checking, rewrites the body into a call of the helper" (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:19`). The rewrite reaches a component's declarations and its traits' and objects' members only (`BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java:54-86`), so a helper string in a local function or an object expression's method stops 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.', where walk answers (row 865). The gather named it among the Effect's departures (`changes.tex`, the Effect of "A native binding that names a static helper"). The manual's rule 4 asks the departing path "a gated XXX test asserting the text's rule" (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "Rules weighed by what they cost against what they protect", 4); the row has reproducer `none`, its test owed as review-routed.1 (`PLAN.md:659`). Climb batch 23's row 849 met the same rule (its finding 8). No library binding sits in either form.

**6. A floating-point division by zero: NaN or infinity (rung F; row 863).** "For floating-point results, division by zero produces a NaN value according to the rules of IEEE 754." (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:167-168`). IEEE 754 gives an infinity for a nonzero dividend; both paths do, and the team's `infinity : RR64 = 1.0 / 0.0` (`Library/Constants.fss:17`) and `tests/realArith.fss:78` rely on it. The row is `CONTESTED`, and no guard asserts a nonzero value divided by zero. F.worker.1 (`PLAN.md:652`). Default: the row as it is.

**7. Question 1: his scope's two sentences split on two bindings (rung S).** His scope named the small rest's "top level 3" and left out "the bindings over `String`"; two of the three are declared over `String` (`CLIMB-BATCH-24.md:76-88`). (`:63`); and two clauses of P-156 (`:67`): "after the switch-over the code generator's refusal of a method with a `where` clause stops it too, as it stops `SumReduction`'s two `distribute`s (row 701)", and, in its Why, "and the code generator refuses a `where` clause in a declaration's header". gather.1 names the first two of P-151 and P-156 and not the Why clause (`PLAN.md:657`; `RECORD.md:296`). #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""words-subset.py APPLY [--allow WORD ...]: check that a scrape only deletes.

For each entry line `- F-87 ...` or `- P-48 ...` of the apply file, compare its
words with the entry as FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md holds it now: every word of the
new line must occur in the old one at least as often (case and punctuation
ignored), so that words can be deleted or reordered but none added. --allow
names words that may be added (default: none). Prints each entry that adds a
word, with the words added, and exits 1 if there is any; new entries (`F-?1`)
are reported as not allowed.
"""
import re, sys
from collections import Counter

ROOT = '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/'
args = sys.argv[1:]
allow = set()
if '--allow' in args:
    i = args.index('--allow'); allow = {w.lower() for w in args[i + 1:]}; args = args[:i]
words = lambda s: Counter(w.lower() for w in re.findall(r"[\w'`\\-]+", s))
old = {}
for f in ('FACTS.md', 'POSITIONS.md'):
    for l in open(ROOT + f):
        m = re.match(r'- ([FP]-\d+) ', l)
        if m: old[m.group(1)] = l
bad = 0; n = 0
for l in open(args[0]):
    m = re.match(r'- ([FP]-[\d?]+) ', l)
    if not m: continue
    n += 1; k = m.group(1)
    if k not in old: print(f'{k}: not an existing entry'); bad += 1; continue
    added = words(l) - words(old[k])
    added = {w: c for w, c in added.items() if w not in allow}
    if added: bad += 1; print(f'{k}: adds ' + ', '.join(f'{w}' + (f' x{c}' if c > 1 else '') for w, c in added.items()))
print(f'words-subset: {n} entries, {bad} add words')
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)

### 4.2 Way 2: the binding's declared types

The binding declares the Fortress types; walk already carries them so (F-299). Two places can give the checker the same reading.

**2a, in the foreign-type table** (`hard-set-way2a-table.patch`). The rewrite records each binding's declared types, `self` first and the result last, keyed by the helper's class and method; `NamingCzar` reads, at a position whose Java type carries the declared type (`int`: `NN32`, `Char`; `long`: `NN64`), the declared type in place of `ZZ32` or `ZZ64`; `ForeignJava` and the wrapper generator `FortressMethodAdapter` pass the class and the position (+85 −13 over four files).

- **What the measurements show.** `ForeignJava` reads every public method of a helper class once per JVM, at the first import of any of them, and keeps that reading (`repository/ForeignJava.java:451`, `:492`). So the reading is that of the first component whose import reaches the class. In the one library, `ZZ32`'s `unsigned` in `FortressLibrary` names `simpleUnsignedIntArith` (moved by climb batch 23), and the class was read before `FortressBuiltin`'s `NN32` `+` recorded its types: the distance 1, at that `+`, read as `(ZZ32, ZZ32)->ZZ32`. With `ZZ32`'s `unsigned` put back on its glue class for one run, and nothing else changed, the distance 0 (runs 2a-1, 2a-2). In the compiler's world, where the prelude's own `import java` reaches the class first, the sample's three bindings fail as on the base, while the wrapper that the same compile writes reads the helper at `NN32`: `javap` shows `unsignedIntOverflowingAdd(FZZ32, FZZ32)` before, `(FNN32, FNN32)` after, and `(FZZ32, FZZ32)` again after the next compile of an unrelated program (run 2a-3). Every compile that builds the foreign api writes the class's wrapper anew (`ForeignJava.java:568`; `compiler/phases/CodeGenerationPhase.java:77-94`; `compiler/nativeInterface/FortressTransformer.java:65`), and the prelude's jar calls the wrapper by its descriptor.
- **Cost.** For the 82: the patch, made order-independent, which needs every binding's types known before any class is read (a pass over the library's text before the graph, or a table written by hand, which is way 1's information kept in the checker), and one reading per helper for every user of it, the prelude's `import java` and any test's included; 82 strings. No new helper; walk no change.
- **Residue at the switch-over.** The prelude's conflict ends with the prelude; the shared wrapper and the first-reader rule stay, so a later `import java` of one of these classes at its default reading, or two bindings that declare one helper differently, break each other. No test program today `import java`s the unsigned or `Char` classes (`grep` over the test folders), and among the 213 bindings of A and B no helper is named at two declared signatures over a carried `int` or `long` (five helpers at two signatures, all among the rest: `doublePow`, `doubleCeiling`, `compareTo`, `nativeConcatenate`, `makeZZfromZZ64`).

**2b, at the rewrite, through the team's transfers** (`hard-set-way2b-rewrite.patch`). The rewrite that turns a bare body into a call of its helper (F-298) reads the declaration's type at each position; where the helper's Java type there is `int` or `long`, the stand-in table reads it as `ZZ32` or `ZZ64`, and the declared type is `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, it puts the matching transfer helper around the argument, or around the call for the result. So `opr +(self,b:NN32):NN32 = builtinPrimitive("...unsignedIntOverflowingAdd")` is checked and compiled as the prelude's text, `makeNN32FromZZ32(unsignedIntOverflowingAdd(makeZZ32FromNN32(self), makeZZ32FromNN32(b)))`. A helper that already reads a position as the declared type, as the six themselves, gets no transfer there. +86 −11 lines in `BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`, nothing else.

- **Cost.** For the 82: the patch; 80 strings, each naming the binding's existing helper (NN32's `asFloat` also needs fork 12's answer; NN32's `CHOOSE` goes through `simpleLongArith.longOverflowingChoose`, `simpleUnsignedIntArith.java:80-82`, which rung K fixes, so it follows K); no new helper; no change of the checker's table, of walk or of the code generator. `FlatString`'s `get` and `javaIndexOf` fit it too, by reading. For the rest of the 109: nothing (no carrier).
- **Residue at the switch-over.** None in the checker: the six names stay what they are now, the transfers that the prelude and the six transfer bindings already use. It binds the six helpers to staying identities: a fix of rows 856 or 857 that makes `signed` or `char` raise must bind them to new checking helpers, not change the six, which the prelude and 2b use as transfers. The compiled code makes the prelude's calls, a binary operation three wrapper calls more than one bare call; F-301 measured that C2 inlines a helper's whole path and removes the temporary box of a helper's result passed into another helper, so by reading the transfers cost nothing once hot (not measured for this composition). The rewrite runs at the parse only on the compiled path's repositories (F-298), so the composition is in no source text.
- **Measured** (runs 2b-1 to 2b-4): the distance 0; a control with two misfits, `NN32`'s `+` naming `unsignedIntLT` and `javaDigit` naming `charToUpperCase`, the distance 2, 'Function body has type Boolean, but declared return type is NN32.' and 'ZZ32->ZZ32 is not applicable to an argument of type (Char, ZZ32).', so the stage checks the composed call; walk's sample OK; walk's suite 695 tests, no failure; the compiled sample in the compiler's world, the same text that fails on the base with 3 errors, links and runs, PASS.

So a subtraction below 0 on `NN32` raises. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators ∔ (`DOTPLUS`), ∸ (`DOTMINUS`) and ⨰ (`DOTTIMES`), fully parenthesised, since the specification states their precedence only among the three. The specification's saturating operators, such as ⊞ (`BOXPLUS`), are not in the interpreter's library; they come in a later step of their own (row 797). Why: this is the specification's rule, and the compiled path already raised the error for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`. The decision is walk's. On the compiled path the rule holds as the specification's (P-25, the standard), and the compiled path departs from it at `^` (rows 523 to 525).

- P-151 **Only the `where`-clause forms that the team wrote down are built: conditional extension, a function's or a method's condition, and `AnyList`'s `comprises` clause.** A `where` clause states conditions on static parameters, and may introduce static variables of its own, as `where [\E\]` does. A trait or object that extends a type under a `where` condition is that type only where the condition holds, and its members are checked with the condition holding (conditional extension). A `where` condition on a function's or a method's own static parameters bounds them. The team's commented-out clause `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]` becomes live, which clears the type error of `AnyList`'s join `||`; its other operations, `addLeft` and `addRight`, move into `List` (row 799). `SUM`'s fusion with `MAX` and `MIN`, the library's fast path for the maximum or the minimum of sums, stays. A method's `where` condition clears four of the fusion's six type errors; for the other two, the team's commented-out generic `distribute` is the fix measured (F-242 holds the measurement: as the team wrote it, it only moves them). Why: a feature with little support in the team's work bends the language beyond what the curator can review. He has such a feature built where the team left enough design intent for it, or where it is on the critical path to running fast compiled. Row 773: the members scoped to the condition, since a member checked under it stays callable where the condition fails. Row 774: walk's half of conditional extension.
